clue.text: New spell calls her up from the grave

indicators.note: giving the words a new spelling means rearranging their letters into a different order

explanation.surface: A necromancer's fresh incantation summons a woman back from the dead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New spell' looks like a fresh incantation, but it tells you to spell CALLS HER UP anew, rearranging its ten letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sepulchral describes things belonging to a tomb, so a gloomy voice seeming to come out of the grave fits.

clue.text: Sport doesn't add up to anything

parts.note: to add up a column of figures is to sum it
with doesn't, not anything is nothing, the circle O

explanation.surface: A sport is dismissed as amounting to nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doesn't add up to anything' reads as 'adds up to nothing': SUM + O, with 'doesn't' and 'to' turning anything into nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Sumo is Japanese wrestling, a sport.

clue.text: Announce time and cost of delivery

parts.note: to post a notice is to announce it publicly
an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: Someone declares the delivery time and its price.
explanation.definitionFit: Postage is the charge paid for delivering mail.

clue.text: Poems with pages that need cutting?

definitions.meaning: Walt Whitman's famous collection of poetry
leaves can be pages, and blades of grass need mowing

explanation.surface: An old book of verse has uncut pages.
explanation.walkthrough: Old books were sold with folded pages that the reader had to slit open, which the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Whitman's volume is a collection of poems, and literally names blades of lawn needing mowing.

clue.text: Didn't show what I show

parts.note: hid is the past tense of hide, to keep out of sight
eh is said when asking 'what?'

explanation.surface: A performer stayed hidden instead of displaying his act.
explanation.walkthrough: HI-DE-HI was a British TV sitcom set in a 1950s holiday camp.
explanation.definitionFit: Hi-de-Hi is the name of a British television comedy series, so it is a show.

clue.text: A worker across the Channel who's taken by aliens?

indicators.note: the bee spreads across the channel, holding it inside

parts.note: a worker is a sterile female bee
a duct is a channel or tube carrying fluid

explanation.surface: A labourer travels to France and is kidnapped by extraterrestrials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'across the Channel' points the solver to France, but here 'across' is the container signal: the worker straddles the channel.
explanation.definitionFit: An abductee is a person carried off, especially in tales of alien kidnapping.

clue.text: Hose slipping into this?

indicators.note: letters that slip out of place end up rearranged, so the four letters of the word hose are mixed

explanation.surface: A stocking-clad foot slides into footwear.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: hose (stockings) slip into a shoe, and 'slipping' shuffles HOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Footwear is what a stockinged foot slips into, which the whole clue describes.

clue.text: Half-chance overcoming each obstacle to progress

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece sits over the other

parts.note: tossing a coin gives a fifty-fifty chance of heads

explanation.surface: A fifty-fifty opportunity gets past every hurdle in the way.
explanation.walkthrough: A head sea is waves running against a ship's course, slowing it.
explanation.definitionFit: A head sea is waves coming straight at a ship, which impedes its progress.

clue.text: Like some species in garden, need moving

indicators.note: letters that are moving shift out of place, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Some wildlife in a garden needs relocating.
explanation.definitionFit: Endangered species are those at risk of extinction.

clue.text: Girl is left locked in, but not to be found?

indicators.note: one piece is shut up inside another, as a prisoner is locked in a cell

parts.note: a maid is an old word for a girl

explanation.surface: A girl locked in a room becomes impossible to find.
explanation.definitionFit: Something mislaid has been put somewhere forgotten, so it cannot be found.

clue.text: Conservative, one proverbially straight, like nails?

parts.note: the saying 'straight as a die' makes a die the proverbially straight thing
the saying 'hard as nails' makes nails the type of hardness

explanation.surface: A Tory is described as upright and as tough as nails.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces come from stock similes: 'straight as a die' and 'hard as nails'.
explanation.definitionFit: A die-hard is someone who stubbornly resists change, the traditionalist sense of a conservative.

clue.text: Greedily get one's oats?

parts.note: pictured as a horse wolfing down its feed of oats

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to eat in huge quantities, as a horse munches its oats.

clue.text: Stay in contention to perform as surgeon

definitions.meaning: in golf, to survive the halfway reduction of the field and keep playing
literally, to make the incision a surgeon makes

explanation.surface: A doctor keeps himself in the running by operating.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means qualifying to continue in a competition, and read literally it is a surgeon's incision.

clue.text: Shiny paper?

parts.note: read as a newspaper whose title names something that shines in the sky

explanation.definitionFit: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper, and the sun is what shines.

clue.text: Flowers I put mulch round less evenly

indicators.note: the compost is put round the other piece, enclosing it

parts.note: compost is spread as a mulch on beds

indicators.note: the even-numbered letters, second and fourth, of the word less are taken

explanation.surface: A gardener spreads mulch around plants but not uniformly.
explanation.definitionFit: Composites are the daisy family of plants, whose flower heads are made of many tiny florets.

clue.text: Wild creature's rude address to Anglican congregation

parts.note: O is a blunt vocative, as in 'O you there'
CE stands for the Church of England, the Anglican church
a lot is a group or crowd of people gathered together

explanation.surface: Someone bluntly addresses a church full of Anglican worshippers.
explanation.walkthrough: Heard together the pieces say 'O, C of E lot!', a rude way to hail Anglican churchgoers.
explanation.definitionFit: An ocelot is a wild cat of the Americas, so it is a wild creature.

clue.text: Rarely make offering to church? Just like Catholic priest

indicators.note: one piece is added to another, placed side by side

parts.note: CE stands for Church of England
to libate is a rarely used verb meaning to pour out a drink offering

explanation.surface: Someone seldom puts money in the collection, like an unmarried priest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rarely' warns that the verb is an uncommon one; libating is pouring a drink offering to a god.
explanation.definitionFit: Catholic priests take a vow not to marry, which is what celibate describes.

clue.text: Initially severe trouble filling in chap's old jumbo

indicators.note: the pieces fill the inside of the other word

parts.note: a chap is a man

indicators.note: only the first letter of severe is taken

parts.note: a to-do is a fuss or trouble

explanation.surface: A man is in serious trouble with his elderly elephant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jumbo' means an elephant here.
explanation.definitionFit: The mastodon was a prehistoric elephant-like animal, so an ancient jumbo.

clue.text: Man dropping in rope to go round area in country

parts.note: a para, a paratrooper, is a man who drops in by parachute

indicators.note: one piece surrounds another, going round it

parts.note: a guy is a rope used to steady a tent or mast

explanation.surface: A parachutist descends on a rope that circles a region of a country.
explanation.definitionFit: Paraguay is a landlocked nation of South America.

clue.text: Keep losing confidence in fortification

definitions.meaning: a stronghold, the inner tower of a castle
a small detached fort or earthwork

explanation.surface: A garrison loses faith in its defences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing confidence in' suggests 're-doubt', doubting again, linking the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: A redoubt is a defensive stronghold, both a keep and a fortification.

clue.text: Swan — observe reflection

parts.note: a pen is a female swan
to observe is to see

explanation.surface: Watch a swan's image mirrored on the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reflection' wants to be the swan's image on water; it means a thought.
explanation.definitionFit: A pensée is a thought or reflection put into words, borrowed from French.

clue.text: Relish welcoming one's rescuer

indicators.note: the word takes the other piece in, as a host welcomes a guest

parts.note: to relish something is to savour it
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Enjoying the arrival of one's rescuer.
explanation.definitionFit: A saviour is someone who saves or delivers others from danger.

clue.text: Poet's handwriting so hard to read, no end

definitions.note: read as 'poet is', so the definition is the poet

indicators.note: the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: crabbed writing is cramped and difficult to decipher

explanation.surface: A poet's script is so illegible it never seems to finish.
explanation.walkthrough: George Crabbe was an English poet of the late 1700s.
explanation.definitionFit: George Crabbe wrote The Village and The Borough, narrative poems of English rural life.

clue.text: Turf accountants do need backers

indicators.note: the backs, or final letters, of the three words that follow are taken

explanation.surface: Bookmakers need people to put money on the horses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turf accountants' is a jokey British name for bookmakers, but 'Turf' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sod is a piece of turf cut out with the grass on it.

clue.text: Father's strange greeting: I'm slapped on the face

indicators.note: something strange is out of its usual order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: ave is Latin for hail, a greeting

explanation.surface: Dad says something odd: he has been slapped across the cheek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' turns FATHERS into AFTERSH, then AVE is added.
explanation.definitionFit: Aftershave lotion is patted onto the cheeks after shaving, so it speaks of itself being slapped on the face.

clue.text: Small daughter a nuisance in bed

parts.note: wee means small, Scottish style

explanation.surface: A little girl is a pest when put to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bed' is a flower bed, not a sleeping place.
explanation.definitionFit: An unwanted plant growing in a garden bed is a nuisance to the gardener.

clue.text: Bound to believe if one's told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: to trust is to believe in someone

explanation.surface: One is obliged to have faith in what one hears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' looks like 'obliged'; it means tied up, as a chicken is trussed.
explanation.definitionFit: Trussed means tied up tightly, as a bound captive or a roasting bird is.

clue.text: First among agricultural buildings, without exception

definitions.meaning: read literally, the number-one farm building
a phrase meaning every single one, with none left out

explanation.surface: The best farm building is the finest of all, no exceptions.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means with no exceptions at all, and literally it names the first of the farm buildings.

clue.text: A Starkadder traced in Somerset House

indicators.note: the letters can be traced within the run of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A family member is tracked down in the old public records office.
explanation.walkthrough: The Starkadders are the farming family in Stella Gibbons's comic novel Cold Comfort Farm. Somerset House in London once held birth and death records.
explanation.definitionFit: Seth Starkadder is one of the brooding family in Cold Comfort Farm, so he is one Starkadder.

clue.text: Ignoring danger, died under tree that fell

indicators.note: a tree that fell has toppled over, so these letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for died, as in family trees

explanation.surface: Someone braved the danger and was killed when a tree came down on him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fell' turns UNDER TREE into UNDETERRE, and D follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone undeterred carries on regardless of the risk, so ignoring danger.
